title: Southern Rhodesia and the Sports Car Club of America
summary: On a State Department tour of Africa the band had no problems in Salisbury, and Benny Morton and he were welcomed at a race meet because of his Sports Car Club blazer.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Mr. Bushell, what other town do you recall visiting that was exciting?

Well, being an auto bug brings to my mind our engagement in Southern Rhodesia, Salisbury, to be exact. You know, that's the country where they have the double standard, you know, one standard for Africans and one standard for the non-Africans. There are signs on all the buildings saying that we reserve the right to exclude whom we wish, meaning that they can throw you out on your ear when they're ready. And there were three blacks in the orchestra. But our State Department had briefed us previously, saying, 'if you have any trouble, that's just what we want, but I don't think they'll do anything.' Which they didn't. We went wherever the white musicians went and we stayed. There were no incidents at all.
But I remember one night Benny Morton -- Remember Benny Morton, the trumbonist?

Well, we went down to the grill to have a sandwich and a glass of beer and there were four or five fellows sitting over in the corner. I had on my blazer with the emblem of the Sports Car Club of America, and they saw that and said, "Hey, you belong to the Sports Car Club of America?" I said, "I certainly do." I pulled out my credentials and showed them. "Come on, have a seat." Well, it turned out, in their minds, Sports Car Club of America -- they have great regard for the Sports Car Club of America. To them it's just the greatest automobile club in the world. And they found out that there was a black American that belongs to the sports car club and they had -- they accepted me with open arms. And sat down and said, "Tomorrow, we're having the -- one of our biggest meets. Would you like to attend? Would you like to come out?" I said, "Certainly would." "All right, see you tomorrow, come out to the gate and just ask for me, or if you forget the name, either one of us -- some of us will be there." Sure enough, Benny And I went out to the race track the next day and one of the -- two of the fellows were at the gate and they drove us back in one of the race cars to their starting tower, you know, and took us up there and introduced us to the judges and what not.
